1	# Fight AI — Backend
2	
3	## Workflow
4	- Always apply changes directly to the local working directory
5	- Never open PRs or suggest creating pull requests
6	
7	## What it does
8	FastAPI service that exposes fight data (fights, rounds, fighter frames, predictions, hand labels) stored by the AI pipeline and the Annotate frontend in PostgreSQL, and spawns/tracks the AI-venv pipeline as a subprocess.
9	
10	## Project Structure
11	```
12	backend/
13	├── app/
14	│   ├── main.py               # FastAPI app + router registration + startup pid reconciliation
15	│   ├── api/
16	│   │   └── routes/

53	
54	## API Routes
55	
56	### `/fights/` router
57	| Method | Path | Description |
58	|--------|------|-------------|
59	| GET | `/fights/` | List all fights (`FightResponse[]`) |
60	| GET | `/fights/stream` | SSE stream of `{id, state}` on every state change (snapshot on connect, then live via `pg_notify('fight_state', …)`) |
61	| POST | `/fights/upload` | Upload a video (`mode=ai\|manual`); creates the fight row (`state='validating'`) and spawns the full-decode validator, which spawns the pipeline itself on success |
62	| GET | `/fights/{fight_id}/rounds/` | Rounds for a fight (`RoundResponse[]`) — AI segmentation output |
63	| GET | `/fights/{fight_id}/frames/` | Fighter bounding boxes + keypoints per frame (`FighterFrameResponse[]`) |
64	| GET | `/fights/{fight_id}/events/` | Pipeline-predicted events scoped to a fight (`FightEventResponse[]`); optional `fighter_id` / `action` / `success` query filters — read-only, never written by the frontend |
65	| GET/POST/DELETE | `/fights/{fight_id}/label-events/` | Hand-labelled strike/state/etc. events (`LabelEventResponse[]`) — the Annotate page's only write path |
66	| GET/POST/PUT/DELETE | `/fights/{fight_id}/label-spans/` | Hand-labelled round/corner_swap/excluded spans; GET auto-seeds `round` spans from the `rounds` table on first call |
67	| POST | `/fights/{fight_id}/finish-labeling` | `labeling_in_progress → labeling_complete`, sets `labeled_at`; 409 if every detected round doesn't yet have a confirmed `round` label-span |
68	| GET | `/fights/{fight_id}/video` | Streams the source video file |
69	| DELETE | `/fights/{fight_id}/` | Kill any running pipeline/validator for this fight, delete the video file, then the row (child rows cascade) |
70	
71	**No route exists to reassign `red_fighter_id`/`blue_fighter_id` after upload** (a `PATCH /corners/` was documented here previously but was never actually implemented — `fighter_service.py` has no corresponding function). If a fight's corners are backward relative to the footage, that's cosmetic only — `label_events.corner`/`fighter_frames.corner` are what training reads, not the fighter-name mapping — but there's currently no UI/API path to fix the displayed names short of a direct DB update.
72	
73	### `/fighters/` router
74	| Method | Path | Description |
75	|--------|------|-------------|
76	| GET | `/fighters/` | List/search fighters (`FighterResponse[]`); optional `search` (ILIKE on names/nickname) |
77	| POST | `/fighters/` | Create a fighter (`FighterCreate` → `FighterResponse`) |
78	| GET | `/fighters/{id}/` | Single fighter (404 if not found) |
79	| GET | `/fighters/{id}/events/` | Cross-fight predicted events for a fighter (`FightEventResponse[]`); optional `action` (prefix) / `success` filters — serves "all jabs fighter X landed" |
80	
81	### Legacy
82	| Method | Path | Description |
83	|--------|------|-------------|
84	| GET | `/events/` | All pipeline-predicted events regardless of fight (backwards compatibility) — read-only, `POST`/`DELETE` were removed once labelling moved to `label_events` |
85	
86	## Models / Schemas
87	
88	### `FightResponse`
89	`id`, `video_path`, `fps` (int), `width`, `height`, `created_at`, `state`, `labeled_at` (nullable), `reported_frames`/`decoded_frames` (nullable — full-decode validation result, populated when `state=invalid`), `segmentation_needs_review`/`segmentation_review_reason` (whether the AI round list was corroborated by the scoreboard — written by the pipeline via `ai/database.py`'s `set_segmentation_review`, never by labelling; drives the Annotate page warning banner), `red_fighter_id`/`blue_fighter_id` (nullable), `red_fighter_name`/`blue_fighter_name` (nullable, joined in).
90	
91	`fps` lets the frontend map video time → frame number.
92	`width` / `height` are the video's native resolution; the overlay uses them to scale bbox coords.
93	`state` is one of `validating|invalid|queued|detecting|tracking|pose|corners|scoreboard|segmenting|analyzing|completed|failed|labeling_in_progress|labeling_complete` — see `frontend/src/types/Fight.ts` for the full state machine and helper predicates (`isFightViewable`, `isLabelingReady`, `isInvalid`).
94	`labeled_at` is the durable "ground truth finalised" marker — distinct from `state`, which resets when a labelled fight is re-run through the AI pipeline to become an evaluation fixture.
95	
96	### `FighterResponse` / `FighterCreate`
97	`FighterResponse`: `id`, `first_name`, `last_name`, `nickname` (nullable), `created_at`.
98	`FighterCreate`: `first_name`, `last_name`, `nickname` (optional).
99	
100	### `FighterFrameResponse`
101	`fight_id`, `frame` (1-based), `corner` (0=red, 1=blue — formerly `fighter_id`), `x1`, `y1`, `x2`, `y2`, `confidence`, `keypoints`
102	
103	### `RoundResponse`
104	`id`, `fight_id`, `round_number`, `start_frame` (1-based), `end_frame` (1-based)
105	
106	### `FightEventResponse` (pipeline predictions — read-only)
107	`id`, `frame` (1-based), `description`, `fight_id`, `fighter_id` (nullable, FK to `fighters`), `action` (nullable), `success` (nullable bool), `state` (nullable — STRIKING/CLINCH/GROUND on a state-change row)
108	
109	### `LabelEventResponse` / `LabelEventCreate` (hand labels — Annotate's write path)
110	`id`, `frame`, `description`, `fight_id`, `corner` (nullable int, 0=red/1=blue — null for state marks), `action` (nullable), `target` (nullable — head/body/leg), `success` (nullable bool — null unless it's a knockdown), `labeler` (nullable), `created_at`
111	
112	### `LabelSpanResponse` / `LabelSpanCreate` / `LabelSpanUpdate`
113	`id`, `fight_id`, `kind` (`round`|`corner_swap`|`excluded`), `start_frame`, `end_frame` (nullable — null means a start/end toggle is still open), `value` (nullable — round number, or exclusion reason), `created_at`
114	
115	## Frame-numbering contract
116	All `frame`, `start_frame`, `end_frame` values are **1-based** (first frame of the video = 1), matching the AI pipeline writer. The frontend converts `currentTime` via `Math.floor(currentTime * fps) + 1`.
117	
118	## Predictions vs. labels — never mix them
119	`fight_events` is pipeline output: `process_fight()` `DELETE`s and rewrites the whole table for a fight on every run, so anything written there is destroyed by the next pipeline run. `label_events`/`label_spans` are hand labels: written only by the Annotate frontend via `label_event_service.py`/`label_span_service.py`, never touched by the pipeline. This split (rather than a `source` column on one table) exists specifically so a query can't accidentally blend model output into training data by forgetting a filter — see plan `0c(5)`.
120	
121	## Upload / validation / pipeline pid handoff
122	`POST /fights/upload` creates the fight row at `state='validating'` and spawns `pipeline_runner.run_validation_async()`, which runs `eval.cli video --fight-id <id>` in the `ai/` venv. That process full-decodes the video, writes `reported_frames`/`decoded_frames`, and either sets `state='invalid'` (truncated file, pipeline never runs) or clears `pid`, spawns `main.py` itself, and writes the new pid — all via `ai/database.py`'s `set_fight_state`/`set_video_check`/`set_fight_pid`, which is why every transition reaches the SSE stream with no backend involvement. `pipeline_runner._AI_ENTRYPOINTS` lists every command-line marker (`main.py`, `eval.cli`) a recorded pid is allowed to belong to — `DELETE /fights/{id}` only signals a pid that's still one of these, so a recycled OS pid can never be killed by mistake. Any new AI-venv job spawned from `pipeline_runner.py` must add its marker there.
123	
124	## Environment
125	- `DATABASE_URL` env var required (PostgreSQL connection string)
126	- `VIDEO_BASE_DIR` — resolves relative `video_path`s and is where `fight_videos/` is created on upload
127	- `AI_DIR` / `AI_PYTHON` (optional) — override the `ai/` venv location `pipeline_runner.py` spawns into; default to `../ai` and `../.venv/bin/python`
128	- `KEEP_VIDEO_ON_DELETE` (dev only) — skip deleting the video file on `DELETE /fights/{id}`
129	- Run with `uvicorn app.main:app --reload` from the `backend/` directory

1	# Fight AI — Python Video Processing Library
2	
3	## Workflow
4	- Always apply changes directly to the local working directory
5	- Never open PRs or suggest creating pull requests
6	
7	## What it does
8	Accepts MMA fight videos, runs ML inference to detect fight events (grappling, state transitions), and writes all results to PostgreSQL. **PostgreSQL is a hard runtime dependency** — there is no no-DB path; the pipeline cannot run without a reachable `DATABASE_URL`.
9	
10	## Project Structure
11	```
12	ai/
13	├── main.py                   # Argument parser + dispatcher ONLY — no business logic
14	├── pipeline.py               # All orchestration logic for both pipeline modes
15	├── debug.py                  # DebugContext — centralised debug output router
16	├── manifest.py               # Builds run summary (returned in-memory, never written to disk)
17	├── video_processing/
18	│   ├── fighter_detection/
19	│   │   └── fighter_detection.py # XL pose model supplies EVERY box + skeleton; the
20	│   │                         #   nano detector (weights.pt) is only a MASK saying
21	│   │                         #   which detected people are the fighters, since
22	│   │                         #   yolo26x-pose is COCO person-only and cannot tell a
23	│   │                         #   fighter from the referee. Nano's red/blue class head
24	│   │                         #   is IGNORED — corner is assign_corners' job.
25	│   ├── fight_segmentation.py # Fuses clock + OCR + detection signals → round list
26	│   ├── round_clock.py        # Fits the scoreboard countdown (slope known a priori =
27	│   │                         #   -1/fps, so only the intercept is estimated) → the
28	│   │                         #   authoritative round COUNT. See "Round segmentation".
29	│   ├── scoreboard_overlay/   # Scoreboard overlay OCR package
30	│   │   ├── __init__.py       # Re-exports + parse_roi_override()
31	│   │   ├── calibration.py    # Bottom-strip OCR to auto-detect overlay ROI
32	│   │   ├── extraction.py     # Per-frame OCR sampling + smoothing
33	│   │   ├── parsers.py        # Org-agnostic round/timer parsing. Two routes to the
34	│   │   │                     #   round: explicit prefix ("R1"/"ROUND 1") and, when
35	│   │   │                     #   the overlay shows a bare digit, box GEOMETRY —
36	│   │   │                     #   find_round_digit_box() locates the 1-char box beside
37	│   │   │                     #   the timer. Calibration unions that box into the ROI,
38	│   │   │                     #   or the crop clips the digit and it is never readable.

88	
89	## Architecture Rules
90	- **`main.py` is a pure argument parser and dispatcher.** It contains no business
91	  logic — only `argparse` setup and a single call to `run_pipeline()` or `run_batch()`.
92	  Do not add conditional logic, file path construction, timing, or imports of
93	  processing modules to `main.py`.
94	- **`pipeline.py` owns all orchestration** via `run_pipeline()` (single-file) and
95	  `run_batch()` (multi-file). Step ordering, skip logic, fallback handling, timing,
96	  and manifest building live here.
97	- **`debug.py / DebugContext`** is the single route for all debug output (images,
98	  JSON snapshots, log lines). Never add scattered `print`/`cv2.imwrite` for debug
99	  purposes — use `ctx.save_image`, `ctx.save_json`, `ctx.log` instead.
100	- **`constants.py`** is the single source of truth for all numeric thresholds.
101	  Never hardcode a threshold or frame-count in a processing module.
102	- **Never change a fight-state or strike-detection threshold in `constants.py`
103	  without measuring it.** This covers the block running from
104	  `FIGHT_STATE_SMOOTHING_WINDOW_SECS` down to `HEAD_ABOVE_SHOULDER_RATIO` — the
105	  `determine_fight_state` classifier and everything `detect_strikes` reads. Run
106	  `python -m eval.cli score <video>` before and after and put both numbers in
107	  the commit message; score's FIGHT STATE and STRIKE DETECTION sections are what
108	  measure these. These thresholds are heavily coupled — several existing values
109	  are compensating for bugs elsewhere rather than describing anything physical
110	  (see `eval/README.md`), so tuning by eye on one video reliably makes another
111	  worse.
112	- **The rule stops there — do not demand a `score` delta for the rest.**
113	  Segmentation (`MIN_FIGHT_END_GAP_SECS` … `ROUND_DISENGAGED_RATIO`) and
114	  scoreboard overlay (`SCOREBOARD_*`) constants are out of scope. Scoreboard OCR
115	  has no `score` section at all. Segmentation does have one (ROUNDS), but its
116	  ground truth is currently untrustworthy: `label_spans` of kind `round` are
117	  **seeded from the pipeline's own `rounds` output** the first time the Annotate
118	  page opens a fight (`backend/app/services/label_span_service.py`), so unless a
119	  human has actually moved those boundaries, round IoU reads ~1.000 against the
120	  prediction itself and a genuine improvement scores as a regression. Check that
121	  the span differs from the `rounds` row before believing a round-IoU number.
122	- **Measure those against the subsystem instead.** A scoreboard OCR change is
123	  validated by timer coverage plus a label-free consistency check: the clock is
124	  linear, so `k = frame/fps + seconds_remaining` is constant within a round and
125	  a misread lands off that intercept. Establish the intercepts from readings the
126	  current settings already accept, then confirm newly admitted readings agree —
127	  that tests for false positives out-of-sample without needing any labels. Note

129	  to the calibrated ROI moves it by a median of 0.117 (max 0.433), and the floor
130	  feeds back into the ROI, since calibration only unions boxes that clear it.

136	```
137	python main.py              # batch mode — scans fight_videos/, processes unprocessed fights
138	python main.py fight.mp4    # single-file mode
139	```

141	### Batch mode (`run_batch`)
142	1. Creates `fight_videos/` if absent and prints a hint, then returns early.
143	2. Scans for `.mp4` / `.mkv` / `.mov`. For each file extracts `fps`, `width`, `height`
144	   via `cv2.VideoCapture` and upserts a `fights` row (`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` — never
145	   disturbs an existing row's state or metadata).
146	3. Queries `SELECT … FROM fights WHERE state NOT IN ('completed', 'labeling_in_progress',
147	   'labeling_complete', 'validating', 'invalid')`. `'failed'` is deliberately included
148	   (retried on the next run); `'validating'`/`'invalid'` are excluded so batch mode
149	   never races the upload validator or reprocesses a file already rejected as truncated.
150	4. Calls `run_pipeline(video_file, fight_id=row.id, …)` for each.
151	5. On success: `set_fight_state(fight_id, COMPLETED)`.
152	6. On exception: logs traceback, continues to next fight (row stays at whatever state
153	   the exception left it in — typically `FAILED`, set by the caller).
154	
155	**Accepted limitation:** a file replaced at the same path is not re-detected by batch
156	(row already exists, `DO NOTHING`). Re-running such a video requires single-file mode,
157	whose upsert resets `state` to `'queued'`.
158	
159	### Single-file mode (`run_pipeline` with `fight_id=None`)
160	Upserts the fight record (`ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET fps/width/height, state='queued'`)
161	so any existing child rows are treated as stale, then runs the full pipeline through
162	`set_fight_state` transitions (`QUEUED → DETECTING → … → ANALYZING → COMPLETED`, or
163	`LABELING_IN_PROGRESS` when `--skip-events` is passed for the manual-labelling track).
164	
165	**Upload validation runs before either mode reaches `main.py`.** The backend spawns
166	`eval.cli video --fight-id <id>` first (state `VALIDATING`), which full-decodes the
167	video, and on a clean result spawns `main.py` itself and hands `pid` off to it — see
168	`eval/cli.py`'s `_validate_and_dispatch` and plan 0b. A truncated file is marked
169	`INVALID` and `main.py` never runs.

171	## Pipeline — fully in-memory data flow
172	
173	**No intermediate data files are ever written.** Each step returns its output dict and
174	the next step consumes it directly. PostgreSQL is the only persistent data store.
175	
176	| Step | Function | Returns |
177	|------|----------|---------|
178	| Fighter detection | `detect_fighters()` | detection dict (XL boxes + keypoints, fighters only, ≤2/frame) |
179	| Fighter tracking | `track_fighters()` | track dict (provisional track_id 0/1) |
180	| Corner assignment | `assign_corners()` | pose dict (class_id remapped to red=0/blue=1) |
181	| Scoreboard OCR | `extract_scoreboard_samples()` | samples dict |
182	| Segmentation | `segment_fights()` | rounds list |
183	| Fight processing | `process_fight()` | — (writes to DB) |
184	
185	`fps` is read once from the `fights` row (extracted from the video at registration time)
186	and threaded in-memory to every step that needs it. No step re-reads fps from disk.
187	
188	**Detection and pose are one step.** They used to be two: a nano detector
189	(`yolov8n`, 3.0M params, 640px) emitted the boxes that survived to the database,
190	and `yolo26x-pose` ran afterwards over every frame purely to have its keypoints
191	copied onto them — its own, much better, boxes were discarded. Worse, the nano
192	box was the *lookup key* for those keypoints (attached only above an IoU floor),
193	so a bad nano box did not merely degrade the box, it dropped the skeleton
194	entirely and the row reached `fighter_frames` with a box and no keypoints.
195	Skeletons are the training signal, so that was silent data loss concentrated on
196	the hardest frames. The XL model now supplies both, and a box and its skeleton
197	can no longer disagree about who they describe.
198	
199	**Developer skip-flags** (`--detection-file`, `--track-file`, `--pose-results`,
200	`--scoreboard-samples`) load a developer-supplied file into the in-memory dict at the
201	appropriate step. The pipeline never *produces* these files.
202	`--reid-file` is a deprecated alias for `--track-file`.
203	
204	**Diagnostic outputs** (`--verify-pose` / `--verify-scoreboard` debug videos and
205	scoreboard calibration debug images) are opt-in artifacts and are not part of the data
206	flow. They remain as explicitly-requested disk outputs and cause `process_fight` to be
207	skipped.

209	## Round segmentation — the clock is authoritative
210	
211	`segment_fights()` combines three signals. **They are not peers** — the order below
212	is a strict authority ranking, and inverting it is what made round counts unreliable:
213	
214	1. **Scoreboard clock** (`round_clock.derive_rounds_from_clock`) — decides the round
215	   **count** and **identity**. The timer is the only deterministic signal in the
216	   pipeline: it advances one second per second of video, so its slope against frame
217	   number is known a priori (`-1/fps`) and only the intercept is fitted, by median.
218	   That makes it robust from ~3 readings anywhere in the round instead of needing
219	   continuous coverage — which matters because broadcast overlays vanish during
220	   replays, corner shots and ground close-ups.
221	2. **Round number** — corroborates the clock and pins boundaries. Nothing may
222	   *depend* on it: plenty of overlays render a bare digit or omit it entirely.
223	3. **Fighter presence + engagement** — refines edges the clock could not pin, and is
224	   the sole signal when OCR fails.
225	
226	**Detection alone cannot decide a round count.** It splits wherever "both fighters
227	visible and close together" fails for `MIN_ROUND_GAP_SECS`, which a ground scramble or
228	a camera cutaway produces routinely. When it is the only signal,
229	`enforce_round_plausibility()` applies physical constraints that need no OCR:
230	
231	- only the **last** round may be short — only the last round can end in a finish, so a
232	  short non-final segment is a walkout or a tracking dropout and is *dropped* (merging
233	  it would drag the real round's start back across the walkout);
234	- gaps below `MIN_ROUND_BREAK_SECS` are detection dropouts inside one round, not
235	  breaks, so the halves are rejoined;
236	- the video must be long enough to hold the rounds claimed.
237	
238	**Edges are only trusted where they were observed.** `ClockRound.start_anchored` /
239	`end_anchored` record whether a reading was actually seen near the top of the round or
240	near 0:00. An unanchored edge is extrapolation past all evidence — a round whose
241	overlay appeared late cannot say where it began, and a round ended by a knockout never
242	reaches 0:00, so clock-zero would fall *after* the fight stopped. `_reconcile_with_clock`
243	takes those edges from detection instead.
244	
245	**The result carries its own verdict.** `quality.needs_review` / `review_reason` say
246	whether the scoreboard actually corroborated the round list, keyed on how many
247	mutually-consistent readings back each round (`ROUND_CLOCK_HEALTHY_SUPPORT`) rather
248	than on raw OCR coverage — an overlay visible 8% of the time still pins its rounds
249	exactly when every reading agrees. `pipeline.py` persists this via
250	`database.set_segmentation_review`, and the Annotate page shows a banner. Without it a
251	detection-only guess reaches the database indistinguishable from a verified one, which
252	is how a 3-round split of a 1-round fight went unnoticed until a human spotted it.
253	
254	`eval/sanity.py` re-checks the same physical constraints label-free, so a regression
255	shows up in `python -m eval.cli sanity <video>` rather than in the annotation UI.

257	## `fight_processing.py` — single-transaction, idempotent write
258	
259	`process_fight(pose_data: dict, fight_id: int, fps: int, rounds: list)` writes all
260	fight data in **one DB transaction**:
261	
262	1. `DELETE FROM fight_events / fighter_frames / rounds WHERE fight_id = :id` — makes
263	   re-running idempotent (no duplicate rows on retry or single-file re-run).
264	2. Bulk-insert `rounds` into the `rounds` table.
265	3. Per-frame loop: collect bbox detections for `class_id` 0/1 into a batch list;
266	   flush every 1 000 rows via `db.flush()` (not `db.commit()`) to release memory
267	   without ending the transaction.
268	4. One `db.commit()` at the very end — either every row lands or none does.
269	
270	The `processed = true` flag update is always the **caller's** responsibility
271	(`run_pipeline` for single-file, `run_batch` for batch), and only runs after this
272	transaction commits successfully.

274	## Frame-numbering contract
275	
276	**Frames are 1-based.** The Nth frame of the video is frame N (first frame = 1).
277	
278	- **Writer** (`process_fight`): `frame_number = index + 1` for `fighter_frames`,
279	  `fight_events`, and round boundaries.
280	- **Frontend** (`FighterOverlay`): `currentFrame = Math.floor(currentTime * fps) + 1`,
281	  using the `fps` returned in `FightResponse`.
282	
283	`fps` is stored as an integer on the `fights` row (`round(cap.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_FPS))`)
284	and is the single source of truth for every frame↔seconds conversion. Never re-read fps
285	from disk or from a video file after registration.

358	## Key Conventions
359	- `LABEL_ID`: `fighter_red=0`, `fighter_blue=1`, `referee=2` (see `constants.py`).
360	  These are **corner ids as written to `fighter_frames.corner`**, decided by
361	  `assign_corners` from appearance — not detector classes. The nano model happens
362	  to share the numbering, but `fighter_detection` collapses its 0/1 into a single
363	  "fighter" concept and never propagates the distinction.
364	- Torso rectangle: built from COCO keypoints `[5,6,11,12]` (left/right shoulder, left/right hip) — primary grappling signal
365	- **Fight-state classification (`determine_fight_state`) is three-way** — `STRIKING` / `CLINCH` / `GROUND`:
366	  - **Proximity axis** — torso-rect distance, normalised by average fighter scale, ≥ `DISTANCE_GRAPPLING_RATIO` (0.11) → `STRIKING`; below it the fighters are entangled (clinch or ground). When the distance or either fighter's scale is unusable (unconfident keypoints), no candidate is read at all for that frame — an unknown distance is never treated as "far apart".
367	  - **Posture axis** (`is_fighter_grounded`) — when entangled, `GROUND` if *either* fighter reads as grounded (knockdown / sprawl / scramble), else `CLINCH`. Primary signal: torso vector tilt from vertical > `TORSO_VERTICAL_ANGLE_THRESHOLD` (50°) — scale-invariant, always evaluated. Backup signal: head→ankle vertical span ÷ fighter scale < `GROUND_VERTICAL_SPAN_RATIO` (1.2) — only used when nose + both ankles are confident and a scale is available, since a hallucinated occluded ankle (routine in a standing clinch) collapses this ratio and misreads GROUNDED while standing.
368	  - **Temporal smoothing** — a majority vote (the categorical equivalent of a median filter) over a `FIGHT_STATE_SMOOTHING_WINDOW_SECS` (0.5s) rolling window of raw per-frame candidates, and a transition only commits once the smoothed candidate differs from the current state **and** at least `FIGHT_STATE_MIN_DWELL_SECS` (0.75s) has passed since the last transition.
369	  - `GRAPPLING_STATES = {CLINCH, GROUND}` is the set that replaces the old binary `GRAPPLING` check everywhere (clinch-strike detection, contact-gate skipping).
370	  - **Strike/state detection only runs inside a detected round** — `process_fight`'s frame loop skips walkouts, between-round rest and the post-fight broadcast wrapper entirely (still writes `fighter_frames` for the whole video, for the frontend overlay).
371	  - **Mid-round replays are also excluded.** `fight_segmentation.detect_replay_ranges()` scans the scoreboard OCR samples for a run of `MIN_REPLAY_SAMPLES` (3) consecutive readings tagged `parse_error = "timer_smoothed_out"` by `scoreboard_overlay/extraction.py`'s `_smooth_samples()` — i.e. the on-screen timer jumped backward relative to the round's established direction, which is what a slow-motion replay clip looks like to the OCR. `segment_fights()` returns these as `excluded_ranges` alongside `rounds`; `pipeline.py` threads them into `process_fight(..., excluded_ranges=...)`, gated in the frame loop the same way as the round check. Requires OCR to actually be calibrating on the source video — falls back to `[]` (no exclusion) when scoreboard detection fails, same as segmentation's own OCR fallback.
372	- **Fighter identity pipeline (two-stage):**
373	  0. `fighter_detection.detect_fighters()`: the XL pose model detects every person in the frame with a box and 17 keypoints; the nano detector supplies a per-frame **mask** of fighter regions, and pose persons are matched one-to-one against it (Hungarian, `FIGHTER_SELECT_IOU_FLOOR`) to pick out the fighters. The referee and cornermen find no mask region and are dropped. Nano's red/blue class head is deliberately unused: it is an independent per-frame colour guess with no temporal consistency, which is the reason step 2 exists. Ignoring it also collapses a real failure mode — ultralytics NMS is class-aware by default, so a fighter the nano model is torn between red and blue on can survive NMS *twice*, as two overlapping boxes; one-to-one matching folds that pair back onto the single person it always was.
374	  1. `FighterTracker` (geometry-only, `models/FighterTracker.py`): constrained 2-slot tracker with IoU + centroid-distance cost matrix solved by Hungarian matching. Assigns a stable *provisional* `track_id` (0 or 1) per frame. Clinch frames (inter-fighter IoU > `CLINCH_IOU_THRESHOLD`) freeze velocity updates to prevent identity swaps. Keypoints ride along on the detection they arrived attached to — there is no box↔skeleton association step left to get wrong.
375	  2. `assign_corners()` (`video_processing/corner_assignment/`): **per-frame appearance-anchored re-ID.** Pass 1 reads the video once, builds per-detection descriptors (glove-tape `net_red`/`tape_total` + torso HSV hue histogram), identifies *clean frames* (fighters separated ≥ `DISTANCE_GRAPPLING_RATIO × avg fighter scale`, both well-posed, tape present), and bootstraps per-corner appearance templates from those frames. Pass 2 (no second video read — over cached descriptors) assigns each detection to a template using normalized tape + Bhattacharyya histogram distance with a hysteresis gate (`CORNER_SWAP_CONFIRM_SECS` converted to frames via the video's fps, consecutive frames before committing a flip). `corner` in `fighter_frames` now legitimately follows appearance across a mid-clinch tracker slot swap. Falls back to a whole-fight paired tape vote / model-class-vote path when template separation is below `CORNER_TEMPLATE_MIN_SEPARATION` (similar colors).
376	
377	     **Verify with `python -m eval.corner_accuracy <fight_id>`.** It is label-free and needs no re-run — it reads the stored `corner` back and checks it against the fighters' kit colour. Corner assignment is the one output with a 50% failure mode that leaves everything self-consistent, so nothing else in `eval/` catches it: `sanity.py` checks structure, `score.py` needs labels, and hand labels inherit the error. Run it on every processed fight; treat `[FAIL]` (whole-fight inversion) and `[WARN]` (intermittent — uncorrected tracker swaps) as real, and treat "no decisive frames" as *unverified*, not as a pass.
378	
379	     **When even the tape vote has too little evidence, corner is UNDETERMINED.** The fallback used to break that tie with the detector's red/blue class vote; `fighter_detection` no longer propagates it, so the mapping is left as identity and logged as unverified. Identity mapping keeps the two corners distinct and self-consistent — it does *not* claim they are the right way round, and a whole-fight inversion looks identical from inside the pipeline. `python -m eval.corner_accuracy <fight_id>` is what catches it.
380	
381	     **Colour is only ever read relatively.** The red HSV band unavoidably overlaps skin, so an absolute red-pixel count is not a corner signal: before this was fixed, *every* fight in `runs/upload_pipeline.log` came back with both tracks overwhelmingly "red", and 29% of a whole `JURICvsNOGUEIRA` frame classified as red tape. 382	     - the wrist crop is sized to the **glove** (`TAPE_PATCH_RATIO`, small forearm multiplier) and gated at `TAPE_MIN_SATURATION = 150`, above the skin band;
383	     - counts are converted to **coverage fractions** of the sampled crop, never summed as raw pixels across the fight — a sum ranks fighters by how long each spent in close-up, which is exactly how `MILIDRAGOVICvsMOOSMAN` was assigned backwards for its whole length;
384	     - the two fighters are compared **within one frame** (they share lighting, exposure and skin tone, so the difference is the part that carries colour) and each frame contributes **one vote**.

386	     **`_is_clean_frame` uses `STRIKING_CORE_KEYPOINT_INDICES`, not `STRIKE_KEYPOINT_INDICES`.** Demanding all 15 strike joints required confident knees and ankles, which a broadcast camera occludes constantly — it returned **zero** clean frames across all 18,518 frames of `NAZHANDvsSTAROPOLI`, so the appearance path never ran and every tracker identity swap went uncorrected. Same relaxation, same reason, as `frame_validity` (see "Frame validity").

Both bugs were live — fight 31 has 755 stored frames with duplicate corner ids. The `Invariant OK: no duplicate corner ids` line at the end of the step is what catches this; treat a `WARNING` there as a release blocker, not a diagnostic.
389	- **Frame validity** — graded via `frame_validity(detections, fight_state) → "FULL" | "PARTIAL" | "INVALID"` in `fight_processing_util.py`:
390	  - `FULL` — both fighters have all strike-relevant joints (head, shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, ankles — `STRIKE_KEYPOINT_INDICES`) above `KEYPOINT_MIN_CONFIDENCE`. Open-range striking runs as normal.
391	  - `PARTIAL` — both fighters detected, below the strict `FULL` bar but with enough of the right joints to run strike detection:
392	    - in `GRAPPLING_STATES`, the per-joint bar is relaxed to `GRAPPLING_MIN_VISIBLE_KEYPOINTS` confident joints — only grappling strike detection (`detect_strikes(..., grappling=True)`) runs;
393	    - in `STRIKING`, both fighters' **core trunk joints** (`STRIKING_CORE_KEYPOINT_INDICES` = head + shoulders + hips) must be confident — open-range `detect_strikes(..., grappling=False)` runs with the full contact gate. The core joints alone give the torso centre, torso rectangle, head centre and scale (everything the contact gate needs from a defender); the attacking arm is gated per-limb inside `detect_strikes`, so a blurred wrist no longer discards the whole frame. **This is what lets open-range punches register** — requiring all 15 joints up front dropped ~95% of standing frames (legs/ankles are routinely occluded in a broadcast view), including the exact impact frames.
394	    - In both cases the per-limb confidence gate inside `detect_strikes` suppresses limbs with occluded joints.
395	  - `INVALID` — fewer than 2 fighters, or joint completeness below even the relaxed bar. Frame is skipped.
396	  - `is_frame_valid()` remains as a thin `FULL`-only bool wrapper for `pose_verification.py` (which has no `fight_state` context).
397	  - **Known limitation:** when the *defender* is fully occluded (1 detection), the frame is still `INVALID` — `detect_strikes` needs both fighters' torso centers. Recovering fully-occluded-defender ground frames is a follow-up task.

399	### Strike detection
400	
401	Strike detection runs in `fight_processing_util.detect_strikes()` on every valid frame and fires for both striking and grappling fight states. All thresholds are **scale- and fps-invariant**:
402	
403	- **Scale reference (`get_fighter_scale`):** torso length (shoulder midpoint → hip midpoint) in pixels, per fighter per frame. Falls back to shoulder width when the torso is foreshortened (torso length < `TORSO_SCALE_MIN_RATIO × shoulder width`) or hips aren't confident. Returns `None` when shoulders themselves aren't confident — the denominator of every normalised threshold below, so `detect_strikes` skips the whole frame rather than compute on a hallucinated scale (see `models/geometry.py`). Used to normalise all distance and velocity thresholds so they are invariant to camera zoom and fighter distance.
404	- **Velocity:** distal-joint displacement against a **per-limb confident baseline** (the last frame in which *that* limb's joints were confident, stored in `strike_state[fighter][limb]["vel_base"]`), minus torso displacement over the same interval (removes locomotion), converted to px/sec (× `fps`) then normalised by attacker scale → `scale/sec`. Compared against `PUNCH_VELOCITY_RATIO` / `KICK_VELOCITY_RATIO`. The baseline is reset when older than ~0.3 s (`max(1, round(fps*0.3))` frames) so a long occlusion never produces a stale spike.
405	- **Contact distance:** normalised by *defender* scale, compared against `HEAD_CONTACT_RATIO` / `TORSO_CONTACT_RATIO` / `LEG_CONTACT_RATIO`.
406	
407	**Three gates must all pass to record a strike:**
408	
409	1. **Extension / angle** — straight arm (angle > `ARM_EXTENSION_THRESHOLD` = 140°) *or* bent arm (`PUNCH_BENT_ANGLE_MIN`–`PUNCH_BENT_ANGLE_MAX` = 60–139°) for punches; straight leg for kicks. The bent-arm path catches hooks and uppercuts.
410	2. **Scale-normalised velocity** — must exceed the ratio threshold for `STRIKE_EXTENSION_SECS` (converted to frames via fps) consecutive frames.
411	3. **Contact proximity** — wrist/ankle must be within the ratio threshold of the target body zone. In grappling mode this open-range proximity gate is replaced by a **directional gate** (see below): a relaxed proximity sanity-check plus a velocity-alignment-toward-target check, because raw proximity no longer discriminates a strike from pummeling once fighters are entangled.
412	
413	**Per-limb keypoint confidence gating:** if any of the three joints (proximal/mid/distal) for a limb is below `KEYPOINT_MIN_CONFIDENCE`, that limb is skipped for the frame. Prevents velocity spikes from hallucinated keypoint coordinates during occlusion.
414	
415	**Keypoint smoothing:** raw pose coordinates are fed through a One-Euro filter (`make_keypoint_smoother` in `fight_processing_util.py`) per joint per axis before any velocity computation. Parameters: `ONE_EURO_MIN_CUTOFF`, `ONE_EURO_BETA`, `ONE_EURO_D_CUTOFF` in `constants.py`. Smoothers are created once per fighter at the start of `process_fight` and persist across frames. Joints below `KEYPOINT_MIN_CONFIDENCE` are passed through *without* updating the filter state — occluded/hallucinated coordinates must not corrupt the One-Euro history and bleed into later frames when the joint reappears.
416	
417	**Grappling / clinch / ground strikes:** when `current_fight_state in GRAPPLING_STATES`, `detect_strikes` is called with `grappling=True` (and `ground=True` when the state is `GROUND`). Lower velocity ratios (`GRAPPLING_PUNCH_VELOCITY_RATIO`, `GRAPPLING_KICK_VELOCITY_RATIO`) are used, the open-range contact gate is replaced by the **directional gate**, and events are emitted immediately. The directional gate rejects wrestling/pummeling false positives: a grappling strike must (a) pass a relaxed proximity sanity-check (`GRAPPLING_HEAD_CONTACT_RATIO` / `GRAPPLING_TORSO_CONTACT_RATIO`) **and** (b) have its end-effector velocity aligned toward the nearest target zone (cosine > `GRAPPLING_STRIKE_DIRECTION_MIN`). Swimming for underhooks, framing, gripping and posturing move the hand laterally or pull it back, so they fall below the alignment threshold. To make grappling detection stricter, raise `GRAPPLING_STRIKE_DIRECTION_MIN` (toward 1.0) and/or `GRAPPLING_PUNCH_VELOCITY_RATIO`. Labels: `clinch_punch` / `clinch_knee` in standing clinch, `ground_punch` / `ground_knee` (ground-and-pound) when on the ground. PARTIAL frames (relaxed joint bar) also run this grappling path.
418	
419	**Velocity uses raw `fps` (not gap-normalized):** `detect_strikes` computes velocity as the displacement from the limb's last-confident baseline to the current frame, multiplied by `fps` — **never divided by the frame gap.** Because the punching wrist blurs and drops below `KEYPOINT_MIN_CONFIDENCE` at impact, those frames are skipped per-limb and the baseline holds, so the displacement naturally spans the blur and captures the full strike. **This is intentional and the velocity thresholds (`PUNCH_VELOCITY_RATIO`, etc.) are tuned against it** — dividing by the gap to get the true per-frame average pushes real open-range punches below threshold and they stop being detected. Do not "normalize" velocity by the frame gap. (The baseline is per-limb and confidence-gated, so it never uses an occluded/hallucinated coordinate — earlier this relied on the strict `FULL` bar guaranteeing a confident previous frame.)
420	
421	**Punch classification (`classify_punch_type`):**
422	- Straight path + lead hand (same side as foot closer to opponent) → `jab`
423	- Straight path + rear hand → `cross`
424	- Bent path + wrist moving mostly upward → `uppercut`
425	- Bent path + wrist moving mostly laterally → `hook`
426	
427	Final open-range punch event type: `{punch_type}_{target}` e.g. `jab_head`, `cross_body`, `hook_head`, `uppercut_head`. Kick types remain `head_kick`, `middle_kick`, `low_kick`.
428	
429	**Head-vs-body target classification (open-range punches):** once a punch is *accepted* (wrist within `HEAD_CONTACT_RATIO` of the head **or** `TORSO_CONTACT_RATIO` of the torso rect — unchanged acceptance reach), the `_head`/`_body` label is decided by the **nearest anatomical region**, not a head-first priority. Each candidate distance is "how far *outside* the region the wrist is" (0 when inside): the head circle (`get_head_radius`, centred on `get_head_center`) vs the torso rectangle (`distance_to_rect`). Label is `_head` when `head_region_dist <= torso_region_dist`, else `_body`. This fixes the prior failure where a head shot landing just outside the point-radius head zone fell through to the torso test and was mislabelled `_body` simply because the head sits directly above the torso rectangle's top edge.
430	- `get_head_center` is **confidence-gated**: it averages only the confident points among nose + ears, falling back to the nose, then to a point `HEAD_ABOVE_SHOULDER_RATIO × scale` above the shoulder midpoint. A hallucinated far ear (common side-on) no longer drags the head centre toward the torso and corrupts the split.
431	- `get_head_radius` uses the ear-to-ear span × `HEAD_RADIUS_EAR_FACTOR` when both ears are confident, else `HEAD_RADIUS_SCALE_RATIO × scale`, clamped to `[HEAD_RADIUS_MIN_RATIO, HEAD_RADIUS_MAX_RATIO] × scale`.
432	- Kicks still use the original head/middle/low priority ladder, but benefit from the improved confidence-gated head centre.
433	
434	**Landed vs. attempted (`RECOIL_LOOKAHEAD_SECS`, `RECOIL_VELOCITY_RATIO`):** for each candidate open-range strike, `process_fight` defers the event write into a `pending_strikes` queue. After `RECOIL_LOOKAHEAD_SECS` (converted to frames via fps) it checks whether the defender's head moved at > `RECOIL_VELOCITY_RATIO × defender_scale / sec` — a proxy for head recoil on impact. The final event description is suffixed with `(landed)`, `(missed)`, or `(unconfirmed)` for strikes at the very end of the video.
435	
436	**`process_fight` signature:** `process_fight(pose_data, fight_id, fps, rounds=None, excluded_ranges=None, red_fighter_id=None, blue_fighter_id=None)` — `fps` is required, sourced from the `fights` row and passed by `pipeline.py`. Strike/state detection is gated to frames inside `rounds` and outside every `excluded_ranges` span (mid-round replays — see above); `fighter_frames` are still written for the whole video regardless.
437	
438	**Event vocabulary in `fight_events.description`:**
439	
440	| Type | Example description |
441	|------|---------------------|
442	| Open-range punch | `fighter_red threw a jab_head (landed)` |
443	| Open-range kick  | `fighter_blue threw a middle_kick (missed)` |
444	| Clinch punch     | `fighter_red threw a clinch_punch` |
445	| Clinch knee      | `fighter_blue threw a clinch_knee` |
446	| Ground punch     | `fighter_red threw a ground_punch` |
447	| Ground knee      | `fighter_blue threw a ground_knee` |
448	| Fight state (clinch) | `Fight state changed to FightState.CLINCH, clinch initiated by fighter_red` |
449	| Fight state (ground) | `Fight state changed to FightState.GROUND, takedown initiated by fighter_red` |
450	| Round boundary   | `Round 1 started` / `Round 1 ended` |
451	
452	Each row also writes the structured columns: `action` holds the strike `type`
453	(`jab_head`, `middle_kick`, `clinch_punch`, …) or an event code (`round_start`,
454	`round_end`, `clinch_initiated`, `takedown_initiated`); `fighter_id` is the
455	attacker/initiator resolved via the corner→`fighters` mapping (NULL for round
456	events or unassigned corners); `success` is True/False for confirmed open-range
457	strikes (landed/missed) and NULL for grappling, end-of-video unconfirmed, and
458	non-strike events.
459	
460	## Environment
461	- `.env` file required with `DATABASE_URL=postgresql://...`
462	- Model weights: `yolo26x-pose.pt` (XL pose — supplies every box and skeleton;
463	  expected in the working dir) and `video_processing/weights.pt` (custom nano
464	  YOLO — used *only* as the fighter/referee mask). Retraining the mask model
465	  single-class ("fighter" vs not) would lose nothing the pipeline uses: its
466	  red/blue head is already ignored.
467	- Videos placed in `fight_videos/` for batch processing

Most Spaces should run out of the box after a GPU upgrade, but sometimes you'll need to install CUDA versions of the machine learning frameworks you use. Please, follow this guide to ensure your Space takes advantage of the improved hardware.

### PyTorch

You'll need to install a version of PyTorch compatible with the built-in CUDA drivers. Adding the following two lines to your `requirements.txt` file should work:

```
--extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu113
torch
```

You can verify whether the installation was successful by running the following code in your `app.py` and checking the output in your Space logs:

```Python
import torch
print(f"Is CUDA available: {torch.cuda.is_available()}")
# True
print(f"CUDA device: {torch.cuda.get_device_name(torch.cuda.current_device())}")
# Tesla T4
```

Many frameworks automatically use the GPU if one is available. This is the case for the Pipelines in 🤗 `transformers`, `fastai` and many others. In other cases, or if you use PyTorch directly, you may need to move your models and data to the GPU to ensure computation is done on the accelerator and not on the CPU. You can use PyTorch's `.to()` syntax, for example:

```Python
model = load_pytorch_model()
model = model.to("cuda")
```

### JAX

If you use JAX, you need to specify the URL that contains CUDA compatible packages. Please, add the following lines to your `requirements.txt` file:

```
-f https://storage.googleapis.com/jax-releases/jax_cuda_releases.html
jax[cuda11_pip]
jaxlib
```

After that, you can verify the installation by printing the output from the following code and checking it in your Space logs.

```Python
import jax

print(f"JAX devices: {jax.devices()}")
# JAX devices: [StreamExecutorGpuDevice(id=0, process_index=0)]
print(f"JAX device type: {jax.devices()[0].device_kind}")
# JAX device type: Tesla T4
```

### Tensorflow

The default `tensorflow` installation should recognize the CUDA device. Just add `tensorflow` to your `requirements.txt` file and use the following code in your `app.py` to verify in your Space logs.

```Python
import tensorflow as tf
print(tf.config.list_physical_devices('GPU'))
# [PhysicalDevice(name='/physical_device:GPU:0', device_type='GPU')]
```

## Billing

Billing on Spaces is based on hardware usage and is computed by the minute: you get charged for every minute the Space runs on the requested hardware, 
regardless of whether the Space is used.

During a Space's lifecycle, it is only billed when the Space is `Starting` or `Running`. This means that there is no cost during build.

If a running Space starts to fail, it will be automatically suspended and the billing will stop.

Spaces running on free hardware are suspended automatically if they are not used for an extended period of time (e.g. two days). Upgraded Spaces run indefinitely by default, even if there is no usage. You can change this behavior by [setting a custom "sleep time"](#sleep-time) in the Space's settings. To interrupt the billing on your Space, you can change the Hardware to CPU basic, or [pause](#pause) it.

Additional information about billing can be found in the [dedicated Hub-wide section](./billing).

### Community GPU Grants 

Do you have an awesome Space but need help covering the GPU hardware upgrade costs? We love helping out those with an innovative Space so please feel free to apply for a community GPU grant and see if yours makes the cut! This application can be found in your Space hardware repo settings in the lower left corner under "sleep time settings":

## Set a custom sleep time[[sleep-time]]

If your Space runs on the default `cpu-basic` hardware, it will go to sleep if inactive for more than a set time (currently, 48 hours). Anyone visiting your Space will restart it automatically.

If you want your Space never to deactivate or if you want to set a custom sleep time, you need to upgrade to paid hardware.

By default, an upgraded Space will never go to sleep. However, you can use this setting for your upgraded Space to become idle (`stopped` stage) when it's unused 😴. You are not going to be charged for the upgraded hardware while it is asleep. The Space will 'wake up' or get restarted once it receives a new visitor.

## Replicas

You can scale your Space horizontally by requesting multiple replicas. This distributes traffic across multiple instances of your Space for improved availability and throughput. You can set the number of replicas via the API:

```
POST https://huggingface.co/api/spaces/{namespace}/{repo}/replicas
Content-Type: application/json

{

```

> [!NOTE]
> Replicas are only available for upgraded (paid) hardware. Each replica is billed independently.

## Streaming Logs, Events, and Metrics[[streaming]]

You can stream real-time logs, status events, and metrics from your Space via SSE (Server-Sent Events):

- **Build or run logs**: `GET /api/spaces/{namespace}/{repo}/logs/{build|run}`
- **Status events**: `GET /api/spaces/{namespace}/{repo}/events`
- **Metrics**: `GET /api/spaces/{namespace}/{repo}/metrics`

These endpoints require authentication and return data using the [SSE protocol](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Server-sent_events).

The logs endpoint accepts an optional `tail` query parameter (non-negative integer) to limit the response to the last N lines of logs:

```

```

## Pausing a Space[[pause]]

You can `pause` a Space from the repo settings. A "paused" Space means that the Space is on hold and will not use resources until manually restarted, and only the owner of a paused Space can restart it. Paused time is not billed.

## Compute

Each service runs on Vercel's compute and is billed the same as [Vercel Functions](/docs/functions/usage-and-pricing): Active CPU, provisioned memory, and invocations. [Fluid Compute](/docs/fluid-compute) applies, so concurrent requests can share an instance.

## Service requests

When one service calls another over a [binding](/docs/services/bindings), each call counts as one service request. Requests that arrive from the public internet are not service requests.

Service requests are [regionally priced](/docs/pricing/regional-pricing), like other Managed Infrastructure resources, and are billed separately from CDN requests. A service-to-service call does not incur a separate Edge Request or Fast Data Transfer charge.

The bytes a service returns are billed as [Fast Origin Transfer](/docs/pricing), the same as other origin traffic on Vercel, whether the response is a static file or comes from a function.

The same [function limits](/docs/functions/limitations) apply to each service, such as memory and maximum duration.

Vercel is a good choice for the frontend. The backend is the hard part, and FastAPI isn't the reason. Your backend also starts the ML pipeline on the same machine and serves the videos from local disk, so wherever it runs, the pipeline runs too.

I timed detection, the slowest part of the pipeline, on your M4:

| Detection | GPU (MPS) | CPU |
|---|---|---|
| 6-min fight (18.5k frames) | 23 min | 4.5 h |
| 20-min fight (60k frames) | 1.3 h | 14.6 h |

It used about 3.9 GB of RAM at peak. Free cloud ARM cores are slower than an M4's, so the CPU column is a best case.

## My recommendation

**1. Start here (almost nothing to move):**
- Put the frontend on Vercel.
- Keep the backend, Postgres and the pipeline on your Mac, and make the API public with [Tailscale Funnel](https://tailscale.com/kb/1223/funnel).
- It's free and keeps the GPU speed. The catch is that the app only works while the Mac is awake.
- Tailscale doesn't publish Funnel's bandwidth cap, but [people stream video through it](https://foundryvtt.wiki/en/setup/hosting/tailscale), and your videos only need 1–3 Mbps.

**2. When it has to be online all the time:**
- Use an [Oracle Cloud Always Free](https://docs.oracle.com/en-us/iaas/Content/FreeTier/freetier_topic-Always_Free_Resources.htm) ARM server: 2 cores, 12 GB RAM, 200 GB disk, 10 TB/month of traffic. That's enough to run FastAPI, Postgres and the videos the way they run now.
- Don't process fights on it; even at best-case CPU speed a 6-min fight takes 4.5+ hours.
- Instead, run the pipeline on your Mac as a worker, or use [Modal](https://modal.com/pricing)'s $30/month free credits (about 50 GPU-hours).
- Status updates already work from another machine, since they go through Postgres. What needs changing is [pipeline_runner.py](backend/app/services/pipeline_runner.py), which starts the pipeline locally, and the local video paths.
- Two Oracle catches: free servers can be out of stock in your region, and a server that sits idle for 7 days can be taken back. Upgrading to Pay As You Go [avoids the takeback](https://oracommit.blogspot.com/2026/02/understanding-oci-always-free-compute.html), and free-tier usage still costs $0.

## What won't work
- **Backend on Vercel:** uploads are capped at 4.5 MB (your videos are 53–474 MB), requests at 5 minutes, and memory at 2 GB.
- **Render free:** it sleeps after 15 minutes, has no permanent disk, and its free Postgres expires after 30 days.
- **Hugging Face Spaces:** new Docker apps now need a paid plan.
- **Cloudflare Tunnel:** the free plan [rejects uploads over 100 MB](https://developers.cloudflare.com/support/troubleshooting/http-status-codes/4xx-client-error/error-413), which is 3 of your 5 videos.
- **Neon or Supabase free databases (0.5 GB):** I estimate each fight takes about 45–145 MB of keypoint data, so your 5 current fights alone would use about 340 MB. I couldn't check the real size because Docker wasn't running.

## Changes needed for Vercel either way
1. **API address:** the frontend calls the API with relative paths that only work through Vite's dev proxy. They're in [api.ts](frontend/src/services/api.ts), [FightList.tsx:39](frontend/src/pages/FightList.tsx:39), [useFightStream.ts:15](frontend/src/hooks/useFightStream.ts:15), and the video players at [Player.tsx:83](frontend/src/pages/Player.tsx:83) and [Annotate.tsx:95](frontend/src/pages/Annotate.tsx:95). Add a `VITE_API_URL` setting.
2. **CORS:** add `CORSMiddleware` to [main.py](backend/app/main.py) so the Vercel site can call the API.
3. **Call the API directly** rather than routing it through Vercel. Vercel cuts proxied requests off at 120 s, too short for a 474 MB upload on most home connections. The videos would also use up the free plan's 100 GB of monthly traffic.
4. **Page reloads:** add a `vercel.json` rule that sends every path to `/index.html`. Otherwise reloading a page like `/fights/12` gives a 404.
5. **Login:** the API has no auth. Once it's public, anyone with the URL can delete fights or upload videos that tie up your machine for hours. Add at least a shared token; the live status stream can't send custom headers, so it needs the token in the URL or a cookie.

I saved these measurements to memory. I also suggested a separate task: `torchreid` is still listed in `ai/requirements-base.txt`, nothing uses it, and it would bloat a deploy image.

Yes, and your code is already most of the way there. Pipeline status updates go through Postgres (`set_fight_state` → `pg_notify` → the live SSE stream), which works the same whether the job runs on the server or on your laptop. The UI already shows `queued` as a waiting state.

## How it would work

```
Browser ─► Vercel (frontend)
   └─HTTPS─► Oracle server: FastAPI + Postgres + video files
                ▲  upload → validate video → state = queued
                │
Laptop worker ──┘  over Tailscale (private network): claim the next queued fight,
                   download its video, run the pipeline, write results, repeat
```

- **Validation stays on the server.** It only decodes the video (OpenCV, no torch), so broken uploads are rejected right away, even with the laptop off.
- **You start the worker when you want** (e.g. `python main.py --worker`). The laptop only makes outgoing connections, so nothing on it is exposed.
- **Fights are processed one at a time.** On your GPU, detection alone takes about 23 min for a 6-min fight and 1.3 h for a 20-min one.

## What has to change

1. **Save the upload mode.** AI vs manual is only passed as a `--skip-events` flag ([fights.py:178](backend/app/api/routes/fights.py:178)), never stored. A worker reading jobs from the database can't tell them apart, so `fights` needs a column for it.
2. **The validator should queue, not start the pipeline.** Today [cli.py:92-104](ai/eval/cli.py:92) launches `main.py` directly. It should set the state to `queued` instead, which also lets the worker listen for new jobs on the existing notification channel.
3. **Don't store the laptop's process id in `fights.pid`.** On startup, the backend marks any fight whose pid isn't a local process as `failed` ([main.py:14](backend/app/main.py:14)), so every backend restart would fail the laptop's jobs. The delete endpoint can't stop a remote process either. If someone deletes a fight mid-processing, the worker's final write fails on the foreign key and nothing is saved.
4. **The worker must look up fights by id.** Single-file mode matches on `video_path` ([pipeline.py:174](ai/pipeline.py:174)). The laptop's downloaded copy has a different path, so it would create a duplicate fight.
5. **Batch the database inserts. This one is easy to miss.** Each `fighter_frames` row is currently sent separately ([fight_processing.py:153](ai/fight_processing/fight_processing.py:153)), one network round trip per row. That's unnoticeable on localhost, but a 20-min fight writes up to ~120k rows. At a typical 25 ms to a cloud server that's about **50 minutes of waiting**, nearly as long as detection. The fix is one line in [database.py:9](ai/database.py:9): pass `executemany_mode="values_plus_batch"` to `create_engine`, which cuts it to about 1,200 round trips (~30 s).
6. **Handle the laptop sleeping.**
   - Database connections can go stale after a long sleep. Add `pool_pre_ping=True` to the engine so the next call reconnects instead of crashing.
   - Run the worker under `caffeinate -i` so the Mac doesn't idle-sleep mid-job.
   - When the worker starts, put back in the queue anything it left half-done.

## Hosting notes
- **Only expose Postgres on Tailscale.** Your [docker-compose.yml:9](docker-compose.yml:9) opens port 5432 on every network interface, which is unsafe on a public server.
- **Upgrade Oracle to Pay As You Go.** With no processing, the server will look idle and could be reclaimed. Usage within the free limits still costs $0.
- **Show whether the worker is online.** A heartbeat lets users see "processing worker offline" instead of a spinner that never moves.

## Your call: who are the users?
There's no login today, and everyone sees every fight.
- **A few people you trust:** a shared invite token is enough.
- **Open to the public:** you'd need accounts, per-user fight lists, and upload limits. Each fight uses up to ~470 MB of video plus ~145 MB of database rows on a 200 GB disk, and your laptop would be processing video files from strangers.

content.text:
You won't need to move the videos. The 20 GB limit I mentioned only covers Oracle's object storage, which I'd use for backups. The server's own disk is **200 GB**, and both the database and the videos live on it. At about 0.43 GB per fight (video plus database rows), that's room for 400+ fights.

Moving videos elsewhere would actually give you less free space, not more:

- **Server disk:** 200 GB
- **Oracle object storage:** 20 GB, about 60 videos
- **Cloudflare R2:** 10 GB, about 30 videos

So it only makes sense if you outgrow the 200 GB.

If you do move them one day, streaming wouldn't get noticeably slower:

- **The videos are light.** They run at 1–3 Mbps, which any of these hosts handles easily.
- **Seeking works the same way.** The browser asks only for the part of the file it needs. Your backend supports that today, and so does object storage.
- **The player needs no changes.** It plays the video in a plain `<video>` tag and draws the overlays from database data, so it doesn't care where the file comes from.
- **The link still goes through your backend**, because login uses a cookie on your own domain. The backend would check the login and hand the browser a short-lived signed link, so the video streams straight from storage.

There are two costs:

- **Deploying adds some lag wherever the file lives.** Scrubbing and frame-stepping will feel a little less instant than on localhost, because every jump fetches data over the internet.
- **Moving the videos adds work.** Uploads would have to go to that storage, and the laptop worker would have to download from it.

So I'd keep videos on the server until space forces the move.
